source.title: The Effect of Intrinsic Dataset Properties on Generalization: Unraveling Learning Differences Between Natural and Medical Images

record.tranche_reason: The study reports generalization results for dataset and representation intrinsic dimensions, but does not test any listed claim version or rely on the claim as a tool.
record.gate_note: The study trains CNNs to fit natural and medical image labels and reports held-out test loss. Its intrinsic-dimension and label-sharpness findings concern related properties, but do not measure any listed version's specific intervention or property. Reported training/test-loss findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study tests generalization scaling with dataset and representation intrinsic dimension and dataset label sharpness. None measures the interventions or relationships in V1–V8. In particular, label sharpness concerns distances between differently labeled images, whereas V7 concerns magnitude-scaled perturbations of model weights.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits adversarial robustness. The authors conclude that intrinsic dimension and label sharpness help describe generalization differences between natural and radiological images, that higher label sharpness is associated with greater adversarial vulnerability in pooled results, and that representation intrinsic dimension is usually approximately bounded by dataset intrinsic dimension. They explicitly leave the causal explanation of the generalization discrepancy unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines supervised CNN generalization scaling with dataset and representation intrinsic dimensions, rather than the interventions or measurements in the listed versions. Models use Adam and are trained to fit the training set.
record.method_sensitivity: Imaging domain changes the reported generalization scaling; the paper also reports results across model architectures, training-set sizes, and intrinsic-dimension estimators.

fits_no_version.finding: Within imaging domains, test loss typically increases with dataset intrinsic dimension; the scaling is steeper for radiological images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization scaling with dataset intrinsic dimension differs between natural and radiological image datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Test loss typically increases with final-hidden-layer representation intrinsic dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned representation intrinsic dimension is associated with held-out loss in the tested CNNs.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation intrinsic dimension is usually approximately bounded by dataset intrinsic dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Final-hidden-layer representation intrinsic dimension usually does not exceed dataset intrinsic dimension in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Including dataset label sharpness improves scaling-law fit for all six architectures, with log-likelihood ratios from 7.6 to 13.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dataset label sharpness improves the fit of the tested generalization scaling law.

fits_no_version.finding: Pooled correlations between dataset label sharpness and FGSM loss penalty are positive for all six architectures at epsilon 2/255. Within natural-image datasets, all six correlations are negative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The association between dataset label sharpness and adversarial loss penalty depends on which imaging domains are pooled.

record.problems: The authors state that they cannot definitively determine whether label sharpness causes the observed generalization-scaling discrepancy; other unaccounted-for factors may contribute. Many scaling results are conveyed through figures, with text describing aggregate trends.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-level per-model points are not separately transcribed because the text reports aggregate trends and the plotted values are not tabulated.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy under the same recipe.
No width sweep beyond the width needed to interpolate.
No fully connected comparator, local-connectivity intervention, or convolution-derived initialization.
Adam is used without an optimizer or tuning-budget comparison.
Batch sizes differ between architectures, but no controlled batch-size comparison or recipe adaptation is tested.
No dropout intervention or comparison involving dropout and weight-decay removal.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
No identification and removal of memorized examples or matched random-removal control.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The cannot_determine row states concern those versions, not whether the unrelated reported trends exist. Appendix C.3 also contains an internal inconsistency: its prose says every architecture has lower loss on task 2, but Table 3 reports higher task-2 loss for VGG-16 and VGG-19. This does not bear on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on random labels or compare natural-label and random-label performance.
Does not sweep width past the interpolation threshold.
Tests CNNs only; no fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
Uses Adam without comparing optimizers or tuning regimes.
Batch sizes vary by architecture, but the study does not compare batch-size effects.
Does not compare dropout settings or dropout removal.
Measures dataset and representation intrinsic dimensions and label sharpness, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness.
Does not identify or remove memorized examples.

rows.subject: six CNN architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, VGG-13, VGG-16, VGG-19; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: trained to fully fit training set
rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out test loss against training-set intrinsic dimension across datasets and training-set sizes.
rows.measure: Test loss/generalization error scaling with dataset intrinsic dimension ddata
rows.value: Within an imaging domain, generalization error typically increases with ddata; scaling is much sharper for medical data than natural data.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation error bars for natural image datasets over 5 class pairs; Figure 2
rows.note: Aggregate textual description across the six architectures; the figure plots individual model, dataset, and training-size combinations.
rows.check: The reported intrinsic-dimension trend is supported, but cannot establish any listed version. Training used Adam for 100 epochs with weight decay 1e-4; fitting the training set is reported rather than demonstrated by training-loss values.

rows.subject: six CNN architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, VGG-13, VGG-16, VGG-19; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: trained to fully fit training set
rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out test loss against intrinsic dimension of final hidden-layer representations.
rows.measure: Test loss/generalization error scaling with representation intrinsic dimension drepr
rows.value: Generalization error typically increases with drepr, in a similar shape as the ddata scaling.
rows.note: Aggregate textual description; Figure 4 plots individual model, dataset, and training-size combinations.
rows.check: The reported representation-dimension trend is supported, but representation intrinsic dimension is not a measure named by any version.

rows.subject: six CNN architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, VGG-13, VGG-16, VGG-19; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: trained to fully fit training set
rows.operation_detail: Compared dataset intrinsic dimension with final hidden-layer representation intrinsic dimension.
rows.value: The authors report that drepr is usually bounded by ddata in practice.
rows.note: The paper describes the upper bound as approximate and says it was usually observed.
rows.check: The authors describe an approximate, usually observed bound between dataset and representation dimensions. This does not measure any listed version; its incompleteness is not a partial result for those versions.

rows.subject: six CNN architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, VGG-13, VGG-16, VGG-19; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: trained to fully fit training set
rows.operation_detail: Related measured dataset label sharpness to held-out test loss scaling across datasets.
rows.measure: Test loss scaling with ddata, accounting for dataset label sharpness KF
rows.value: Log likelihood ratios favor the model accounting for KF for all six architectures: ResNet-18 13.5; ResNet-34 7.6; ResNet-50 11.7; VGG-13 8.1; VGG-16 10.5; VGG-19 12.3.
rows.note: These are likelihood comparisons for fitted scaling-law models, not direct tests of a causal effect of KF.
rows.check: The six log-likelihood ratios are transcribed correctly. They compare fitted scaling-law models, rather than directly measuring a listed behavioral effect or establishing a causal effect of label sharpness.

rows.subject: six CNN architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, VGG-13, VGG-16, VGG-19; aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: trained to fully fit training set
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-loss penalty from FGSM attacks against dataset label sharpness.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between test-loss penalty and measured label sharpness K̂F
rows.note: This measures adversarial loss penalty, not the train-test generalization gap.
rows.check: The six correlations at epsilon 2/255 are correct for the pooled datasets. They measure adversarial loss penalties against dataset label sharpness, not magnitude-aware weight sharpness against the generalization gap. They do not establish the same association within each domain.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
